content:
President Trump traveled to San Antonio, Texas on Wednesday to campaign for Republican Texas Senate candidate Ken Paxton. The controversy has continued to escalate after Trump made multiple recent comments about Paxton's appearance.

The New York Times on September 30 revealed a leaked recording in which Paxton privately complained that Trump's speech at a Republican midterm election event in Dallas could hurt his campaign. These remarks brought the issue back into the spotlight.

The president himself has yet to respond to the recording.

Last week, while campaigning for him in Denton, Texas, Trump described Paxton as "sometimes really troublesome" and questioned whether he was even in attendance (Paxton was, in fact, present), before later backtracking and calling him "the best attorney general in the country."

On the final night of the Republican midterm election event on September 10, Trump said: "I told him, 'Ken, I don't want to embarrass you, but we have so many disagreements... I don't know if I like your look, I don't know if I like your clothing, I don't like the way you talk.'"

The night before, Trump had said: "(Paxton) may not dress well enough, may not give the perfect speech, and may not be the most handsome person I've ever seen."

In early September, speaking from the Oval Office about Paxton's Democratic opponent James Talarico, Trump said: "We have a guy named Ken Paxton. Some people don't like his clothing, some people don't like the way he gives interviews, and some people don't like the way he talks."

With less than five weeks until the November midterm elections, the Texas Senate race remains tight. According to the latest poll released on October 3 by The New York Times and Siena College, Paxton trails Talarico by six percentage points.

Trump's comments about Paxton's appearance appear to have become a recurring pattern.

Dan Cassino, a political science professor at Fairleigh Dickinson University, told The Huffington Post that Trump has consistently equated masculine physical attributes with strong leadership.

Cassino noted: "At its core, the issue is that Trump has a very clear set of standards for what a good candidate should be and look like. In his mind, the ideal candidate is male, tall, handsome, and dressed in a way that matches his own thinking. If you don't fit that mold, or fall short of that stereotype in any way, Trump considers you an unfit candidate."

Trump also frequently comments on his own appearance. Speaking in Nebraska on Monday, Trump claimed that supporters had told him he looked so good he could be said to have more presidential presence than former presidents George Washington and Abraham Lincoln.

During his first presidential term in 2016, he once asked a crowd: "I think I have a very big presidential aura. Do I look like a president? I think I look like a president... Am I very handsome?"

According to Cassino: "When Trump endorses someone or campaigns alongside them, and that person doesn't meet his standards, this mentality becomes a problem. What he's saying (about Paxton) reflects his belief that Paxton isn't masculine enough, and therefore doesn't look like a good candidate or someone who can win."

Is Trump deliberately making these comments about Paxton?

Brandon Rottinghaus, a political science professor at the University of Houston, believes Trump may be laying the groundwork in case Paxton loses.

Rottinghaus noted: "Ultimately, the question is: who takes the blame? The president may be setting up a scenario where Paxton has to shoulder the responsibility for a potential loss in the state. Trump doesn't want to be the one everyone points to as the person who caused Republican losses."

However, Rottinghaus emphasized that this is only his personal speculation.

He said: "The president's strategy has always been hard to gauge, because he tends to speak off the cuff on these issues. Paxton needs Trump's endorsement and support, and Trump is also happy to make Paxton a laughingstock."

Josh Blank, director of the Texas Politics Project at the University of Texas at Austin, offers two alternative interpretations. The first is that these comments may simply reflect his frustration with the trouble Paxton has caused for the Republicans.

Blank told The Huffington Post: "If the president is overly focused on Ken Paxton's negative traits, it could simply be an expression of frustration."

Another possibility is that these comments give voters a trivial, harmless flaw to focus on, "so that voters can acknowledge his shortcomings while still forgiving themselves for continuing to support him."

Throughout his political career, Paxton has faced multiple charges, including securities fraud, corruption, bribery, abuse of power, and retaliation against whistleblowers. Blank also noted that Paxton has consistently refused to debate Talarico.

Blank said: "This isn't a normal election. If Republicans start behaving strangely in the final months of the campaign, it's because they're not used to being in this position."

Cal Jillson, a political science professor at Southern Methodist University who specializes in Texas politics, believes Paxton's base will very likely continue to support him.

Speaking about Paxton, Jillson said: "I was chatting with an old friend yesterday, and he said: 'You know, he's a con man, but he's our con man.' That perfectly sums up how the Republican base feels."

Why does this election matter?

Paxton is extremely well-known in Texas. After serving in the state legislature for a decade, he was elected attorney general in 2014. Since 2016, he has been a staunch backer of the Great America (Make America Great Again, MAGA) movement, and has received millions of dollars in campaign donations through a Texas-based new political action committee linked to Senate Majority Leader John Thune, MAGA Inc., and other Republican groups.

Jillson pointed out that a loss would have broader implications. "If Paxton loses, and the governor's race is also extremely, extremely close, the consequences will be catastrophic."

As of the time of publication, Paxton's team had not responded to The Huffington Post's interview request.

Zack Kraft, a spokesperson for the Republican National Committee, replied to The Huffington Post's inquiry: "President Trump has called Ken Paxton the strongest attorney general ever, and has made clear that he will do everything in his power to help him become the next Texas U.S. Senator. As Texans learn more about James Talarico's radical agenda—eliminating the oil and gas industry, raising taxes, and forcing gender transitions on children—they will increasingly realize that they absolutely do not want to have anything to do with this person."
